summary: Defines the SIP History-Info header field, which records how and why a request reached a given application or user. This supports services such as voicemail and call distribution. It also defines related header parameters and a Privacy value to anonymize the information.

plainLanguage.summary: The History-Info header field is an optional part of a SIP request that keeps a record of every change of address along the way. It tells the application that finally answers the call which address was called first, why the request was sent elsewhere, and how each new address was chosen. It supports services such as voicemail and call distribution.

questions: how to know why a sip call was redirected
what do rc mp and np mean in history-info
how does sip history-info privacy work
subtitle: A SIP header that records how and why a call reached the application that answered it.

tldr.problem: When a SIP request is retargeted, the original target and the reason for the change are lost, so the application that finally receives the request cannot tell how it got there.
tldr.mechanism: Every proxy or user agent that changes the target appends an entry to a History-Info header field, and each entry carries a dotted index that turns the history into a tree of branches.
tldr.outcome: This version replaces RFC 4244. It adds rc, mp and np parameters that record how each new target was chosen, marks gaps in the history with a zero, and anonymizes entries instead of dropping them when privacy is requested.

today: RFC 7044 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the current definition of the History-Info header field. It replaced RFC 4244, which defined the same header field without the rc, mp and np parameters.

sections.title: Why a Request Needs a History
sections.content:
Many services that SIP is anticipated to support need to know why and how a SIP request arrived at a specific application. The RFC names sessions started by clicking a call-to-talk link on a web page, call history and logging services inside call management software for SIP user agents, and calls to voicemail servers.

SIP already allows a request to be routed to a chosen application, but in the process of retargeting a request, old routing information can be forever lost. That lost information may be important history that allows the element to which the request is retargeted to process it in a locally defined, application-specific manner.

The RFC compares this with what other protocols already offer: web referral applications that let a site learn which associate site sent the visitor, email relaying where the recipient can see the trace of the path of the message including the time of each relay, and traditional telephony services such as voicemail, automatic call distribution and follow-me services. Request history could also improve basic SIP functionality by giving diagnostic information for debugging, by capturing aliases and Globally Routable User Agent URIs that a registrar may overwrite, by facilitating limited use addresses and sub-addressing, and by preserving service-specific URIs that a downstream proxy could overwrite.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP can send a request to a different address than the one that was first dialled, and each change overwrites the last one. The application that answers then has no idea what the original address was or why the request was moved. This document defines a standard way to carry that record along with the request.

sections.title: How History-Info Is Carried
sections.content:
The fundamental function of request history information is to inform proxies and user agents involved in processing a request about the history or progress of that request. The solution is to capture the Request-URIs, as a request is retargeted, in a SIP header field called History-Info.

The header field is added to a request when a new request is created by a User Agent Client, or forwarded by a proxy, or when the target of a request is changed. The same proxy or SIP intermediary may change the target more than once before forwarding, which the RFC calls internal retargeting. A SIP entity that changes the target in response to a redirect also propagates any History-Info header field from the initial request in the new request.

The header field is used in out-of-dialog requests or initial requests for a dialog, such as INVITE, REGISTER, MESSAGE, REFER, OPTIONS, PUBLISH and SUBSCRIBE, and in any non-100 provisional or final responses to those requests. A SIP option tag, histinfo, tells other elements that the sender supports the mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Every element that changes where a request is going appends one entry to a header called History-Info. The entries travel with the request from the first proxy to the last, and a copy of them is also returned in the response when the caller asked for it.

sections.title: The Header Field Syntax
sections.content:
The header field is defined in ABNF as History-Info = "History-Info" HCOLON hi-entry *(COMMA hi-entry), where each hi-entry is a hi-targeted-to-uri followed by zero or more parameters. The hi-targeted-to-uri is a name-addr, the same form used in the Contact header field, and it is the mandatory parameter that captures the Request-URI for the request as it is forwarded.

Each entry also carries a mandatory hi-index, a sequence of nonnegative integers separated by dots that indicates the number of forward hops and retargets. This results in a tree representation of the history of the request, with the lowest-level index reflecting a leaf. An optional hi-target-param records the mechanism by which the Request-URI was determined. An optional hi-extension allows future extensions, and as required by RFC 3261, an implementation that does not understand an extension MUST ignore it.

An hi-entry may also include a Reason header field and a Privacy header field, both included in the headers component of the hi-targeted-to-uri. The Reason reflects information received in a response to the request sent to that URI. Because both fields sit inside the hi-targeted-to-uri, they are not available when the hi-targeted-to-uri is a Tel-URI.
sections.plainLanguage: Each history entry names one address the request was sent to, carries a numbered position, and may carry a note about how that address was chosen. The position is a dotted number such as 1.1.2, where each dot marks another hop or branch.

sections.title: Handling History-Info in Requests and Responses
sections.content:
When receiving a request, a SIP entity MUST keep a copy of the hi-entries from the incoming request in a cache, adding them in the order in which they were received. If the Request-URI of the incoming request does not match the hi-targeted-to-uri in the last hi-entry, which means the previous entity did not include a History-Info header field, the SIP entity MUST add an hi-entry to the end of the cache on behalf of that previous entity, setting the hi-targeted-to-uri to the Request-URI, applying privacy if required, setting the hi-index, and NOT including an rc, mp or np parameter.

When sending a request, the SIP entity MUST include all the hi-entries from the cache and MUST add a new hi-entry to the outgoing request, although it does not add that new entry to the cache at this point. The entries in the outgoing request represent the preorder of the tree, that is, the lexicographic ordering of the hi-indexes.

When a non-100 response arrives or a request times out, the entity adds the hi-entry of the request that got that response to the cache, in ascending order of hi-index, and adds a Reason header field carrying the SIP response code when the response is neither 100 nor 2xx. A timeout is treated as if the request received a SIP error response code of 408 Request Timeout. Any hi-entries received in the response that are not already cached are also added. The cache does not contain hi-entries for requests that have not yet received a non-100 response, so there can be gaps in the indices, for example 1.2 and 1.4 present but not 1.3.

When sending a response other than a 100, a SIP entity MUST include all the cached hi-entries, subject to the privacy rules, except that if the received request contained no hi-entries and there is no histinfo option tag in the Supported header field, it MUST NOT include History-Info in the response.
sections.plainLanguage: Each element keeps a list of the history entries it has seen. When it forwards a request it copies that list and adds one new entry for the address it is sending to. When a response or a timeout comes back, it adds the matching entry to its list and notes the reason. When it answers, it returns the whole list to the caller.

sections.title: Anonymizing the History
sections.content:
The hi-targeted-to-uris in the History-Info header field can inadvertently reveal information about the initiator of the request, so the Privacy header field is used to indicate that privacy must be applied. The RFC defines a new priv-value for it, history. A user agent client that includes a priv-value of header SHOULD NOT also include a priv-value of history. A user agent client that includes any priv-values other than header MUST also include history. A user agent client that includes no priv-values at all MUST add a Privacy header field with a priv-value of history, and MUST NOT include a priv-value of critical in that case.

An intermediary that wants to protect routing information it adds MUST construct a Privacy header field with the single priv-value of history and put it in the hi-targeted-to-uri of each new entry it wants protected. A user agent server that does not want to reveal the final reached target MUST include a Privacy header field with a priv-value of history in the hi-targeted-to-uri of the last entry in the response.

When a message is forwarded to a domain the intermediary is not responsible for, a Privacy Service at the domain boundary applies the privacy. All the hi-targeted-to-uris for that domain are anonymized to URIs containing a domain of anonymous.invalid, and the URI username SHOULD be anonymous. The Privacy header field value is then removed from the hi-entry, and the priv-value of history is removed from the Privacy header field in the message header. If no priv-values remain, the Privacy header field itself is removed. Compared with RFC 4244, entries are anonymized rather than recommended for removal.
sections.plainLanguage: The addresses in the history can reveal who made the call, so a sender can ask for them to be hidden. The element at the edge of a domain replaces the addresses with anonymous ones before passing the request on. This version replaces the old advice to delete the entries with the stronger step of anonymizing them.

sections.title: Indexing the History as a Tree
sections.content:
To maintain ordering and reflect retargeting accurately, the SIP entity MUST add an hi-index to each hi-entry. The hi-index consists of nonnegative integers separated by dots, for example 1.1.2. Each dot reflects a SIP forwarding hop, and the integer after each dot reflects the order in which a request was retargeted at that hop. The highest integer at each hop reflects the number of entities to which the request has been retargeted at that hop, that is, the number of branches. The indexing therefore gives a logical tree representation of the history, and the hi-entries are given in the preorder of the tree.

The first index in a series of History-Info entries MUST be set to 1. When forwarding a request without changing the target, the entity reads the value from the received header field and appends a dot and an initial value of 1 for the new level, so a last index of 1.1 becomes 1.1.1. For each subsequent retargeting by the same entity, the rightmost value is incremented, so the next request forwarded by the same entity gets 1.1.2. Retargeting based on a response, such as a 302, also increments the rightmost value, so an index of 1.2 becomes 1.3. When a request is forked, each fork gets its own index, assigned sequentially, so a last index of 1.1 gives 1.1.1 for the first fork, 1.1.2 for the second, and so on.

If the request clearly has a gap, the entity adding an entry MUST add a single index with a value of 0 before adding the appropriate index, so a last index of 1.1.2 with a missing entry becomes 1.1.2.0.1. Applications MUST be prepared to process messages whose entries show gaps, MUST NOT treat gaps as an error, and SHOULD indicate the gaps to applications.
sections.plainLanguage: The position of each entry is a dotted number, and the numbers form a tree. A new branch gets the next number at that level, and a branch that goes one hop deeper gets one more number added. When the history is known to be incomplete, a zero is inserted to mark the hole.

sections.title: Tagging How the Target Was Determined
sections.content:
This specification defines three header field parameters, rc, mp and np, which appear both in the History-Info header field and in the Contact header field. The parameters rc and mp indicate the mechanism by which a new target for a request is determined, and np reflects that the target has not changed. All three contain an index whose value is the hi-index of the entry with the hi-targeted-to-uri that represents the Request-URI that was retargeted.

The rc parameter applies when the Request-URI has changed while the target user associated with the original Request-URI has been retained, for example when a user has multiple address-of-records as an alias. The mp parameter applies when the target was determined by mapping to a user other than the target user associated with the Request-URI being retargeted, for example when a request is statically or dynamically retargeted to another user represented by an address-of-record unassociated with the original one. The np parameter applies when the target has not changed and the associated Request-URI remained the same, for example when a proxy merely forwards a request to a next-hop proxy and loose routing is used.

There are two ways an mp value can be derived. The mapping may have been done by the receiving entity on its own authority, in which case the mp-value is the parent index of the entry's own index. Or the mapping may have been done because of a received 3xx response, in which case the mp-value is an earlier sibling or a descendant of an earlier sibling, and is the index of the downstream request that received the 3xx response. The np parameter is not applicable in the case of redirection, because the redirect server is the only element with knowledge of how the target was determined, and if the Contact header field carries no rc or mp parameter, the entity MUST NOT add one to the entry.
sections.plainLanguage: Three short tags say why the target changed. rc means the address changed but it is still the same person, for example another of their addresses. mp means the request was sent to a different person entirely. np means the address did not change at all, only the next hop.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC strongly RECOMMENDS the use of the Transport Layer Security protocol as a mechanism to ensure the overall confidentiality of the History-Info header fields. If TLS is NOT used, the intermediary MUST ensure that messages are only sent within an environment that is secured by other means, or that the messages do not leave the intermediary's domain. With TLS, History-Info header fields are no less, nor no more, secure than other SIP header fields inserted by intermediaries.

The RFC notes that using the SIPS scheme protects History-Info from tampering by arbitrary parties outside the SIP message path, but all the intermediaries on the path are trusted implicitly. A malicious intermediary could arbitrarily delete, rewrite or modify History-Info, and this specification does not attempt to prevent or detect attacks by malicious intermediaries.

Appendix A.1 lists the security problems: a rogue application could insert a bogus entry by adding one as a result of retargeting or by entering invalid information, could rearrange the information to change the nature of the end application or mislead the receiver, or could delete some or all of it. The resulting requirements are that the receiver must be able to determine whether previously added content has been altered, that the ordering must be preserved at each instance of retargeting, that the receiver must be able to authenticate the entity providing the request, and that only entities that process the request should have visibility of the information. Appendix A.2 adds the privacy requirements: the entity retargeting the request must maintain the network-provided privacy, the receiver must maintain the privacy associated with the information, and request history subject to privacy must not be included in outgoing messages unless it is protected as described in RFC 3323.
sections.plainLanguage: The history can show where a call has been, so it should travel over an encrypted connection. The document also says plainly that it cannot stop a proxy on the path from rewriting or deleting the history, and it asks for TLS or an equally protected network path.

messages.label: INVITE sip:bob@biloxi.example.com;p=x
messages.note: Alice's proxy starts the history with index=1.

messages.label: INVITE sip:bob@biloxi.example.com;p=x
messages.note: Target unchanged, so the entry is np=1;index=1.1.

messages.label: INVITE sip:bob@192.0.2.3
messages.note: First fork of the contact list: index=1.1.1;rc=1.1.

messages.label: INVITE sip:bob@192.0.2.7
messages.note: Second fork of the contact list: index=1.1.2;rc=1.1.

messages.label: 200 OK
messages.note: The 200 OK carries the cached history entries back.

viz.caption: ABNF OF THE HISTORY-INFO HEADER FIELD AND ITS PARAMETERS

data.title: History-Info grammar
data.code:
History-Info = "History-Info" HCOLON hi-entry *(COMMA hi-entry)

hi-entry = hi-targeted-to-uri *(SEMI hi-param)

hi-targeted-to-uri = name-addr

hi-param = hi-index / hi-target-param / hi-extension

hi-index = "index" EQUAL index-val

index-val =  number *("." number)

number =  [ %x31-39 *DIGIT ] DIGIT

hi-target-param = rc-param / mp-param / np-param

rc-param = "rc" EQUAL index-val

mp-param = "mp" EQUAL index-val

np-param = "np" EQUAL index-val

hi-extension = generic-param

items.label: Retargeted, same user
items.desc: The Request-URI changed while the target user associated with the original Request-URI was retained.

items.label: Mapped to another user
items.desc: The target was determined by a mapping to a user other than the target user of the Request-URI being retargeted.

items.label: No change
items.desc: The target has not changed and the associated Request-URI remained the same.
